AfriScan · Uganda · Secure your land from the air, remotely

Know what has changed inside your corridor in Uganda

AfriScan maps structures, excavations, tracks, cleared ground and vegetation along pipelines, transmission lines, roads, railways and fibre routes, and inside oil, mining and industrial sites. Each result is measured against your right-of-way and wayleave widths, checked by a person, and delivered as GIS files and a PDF report. Satellite first, with no drone approvals needed to start.

The law behind the register Constitution art. 26 · Land Acquisition Act (Cap. 235) · Petroleum (RCTMS) Regulations 2016, regs 68, 87, 91–98 · Electricity Act ss.67–71 · Roads Act 2019 ss.15–17, 24 · S.I. 53 of 2026 · National Environment Act 2019 s.53 · S.I. 96 of 2022 · Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019

The law already sets the lines

The bands your register is measured against

Uganda’s rules draw clear lines around linear assets. What asset owners need is a dated, measured record of what stands inside each band, and since when. That is what we provide.

Midstream Regulations 2016

Pipelines: 6 m, 30 m and the land next to the line

No one may carry out “any activity in an area adjacent to a pipeline system” without PAU’s written consent (reg 68). Anyone planning work within 30 m of a pipeline right of way must first find out where the pipe is (reg 92), and machines may dig within 6 m only under the licensee’s supervision (reg 97). Licensees survey their routes every six months (reg 87(7)).

Read

Electricity Act · UETCL

Power lines: a corridor where nothing is built

A licensee may place lines over any land, paying “prompt, fair, and adequate compensation” for the right of use (Electricity Act s.67). UETCL’s published resettlement framework for a new 400 kV interconnector sets a 60 m corridor with no structures, and vegetation and crops no higher than 2 m. The width is set project by project.

Read

Roads Act 2019

Roads: no compensation for unauthorised structures

“A person who constructs any structure in or on a road reserve … without authorisation … is not entitled to any compensation” (s.16(8)). The Act also provides for building lines (s.17), and the 2026 road regulations set maximum reserve widths by road class. So the date a structure first appeared matters.

Read

Constitution, art. 26

Compensation before possession

Compulsory acquisition needs “prompt payment of fair and adequate compensation, prior to the taking of possession” (art. 26(2)(b)(i)). A dated record of what stood where supports the cut-off date, the valuation and every later grievance check.

Read

Next to a pipeline Work within 30 m of the right of way only after finding the pipe; machines within 6 m only under the licensee’s supervision; where there is no pipeline right of way, no ground disturbance within 6 m without approval 6 m and 30 m S.I. 36 of 2016, regs 91, 92 and 97
Petroleum facilities A safety zone around each facility, set by PAU Set by PAU Midstream Act 2013 s.67; EDP Act 2013 s.144
A new 400 kV line A 10 m right of way acquired outright and 25 m of wayleave each side, registered as an easement 60 m, project-specific UETCL resettlement framework, January 2026
Road reserves Maximum widths by road class, from 10 m on park and community access roads to 40 m on expressways Up to 10–40 m by class S.I. 53 of 2026, Sch. 12
Lakeshores and river banks Land up to 100 m bordering a lake, and a river bank up to 100 m; the Minister may declare protected zones Up to 100 m National Environment Act 2019 s.53
Aerodromes (drones) No drone within 4 km without the aerodrome’s and the air navigation service provider’s written permission and UCAA approval 4 km S.I. 96 of 2022, reg 52

A summary of public rules as of 27 September 2026, for orientation. It is not legal advice; the sources are linked.

Why it matters

What changes between one survey and the next

Pipelines are entering decades of operation, new transmission lines are being prepared, and land for a new railway is being acquired. The land beside them keeps changing.

“The line is going into operation.”

A buried pipeline is a right of way to keep clear for decades. Reinstated ground is easy to farm and build on again, and the six-monthly route survey needs a record of what has changed.

“The wayleave was paid for. Now there is a house in it.”

A structure inside a registered wayleave is easier to discuss while it is new. A dated register shows whether it stood there before the cut-off date or appeared after it.

“When did that building go up?”

On road reserves the date matters as evidence, because the Roads Act denies compensation for structures built in a reserve without authorisation. Archive imagery shows roughly when a structure first appeared, and the register records it against the reserve width.

“We cannot send a team along the whole route.”

Long corridors cross farmland, wetlands and growing towns. Satellite mapping covers all of it with no one on site, so field teams go first to the stretches that changed.

UETCL’s own Grid Development Plan 2025–2040 records that “acquisition of way leaves for construction of transmission lines continues to be a challenge”. A dated register does not settle a wayleave. It gives everyone, the utility, the land team and the occupants, the same record of what stood where and when.

What you receive

A register your land, integrity and GIS teams can use

  • Features by band and by segment: structures, excavations, tracks and cleared ground, sorted into your bands (for example 0–6 m, 6–30 m and beyond 30 m of a pipeline) and into 500 m stretches rated for encroachment density.
  • Distance and position: each feature’s distance to the centreline, its chainage and its coordinates in WGS84 and in the route’s UTM zone.
  • A date for every feature: the imagery named, with its capture date where the source gives one.
  • Change since the last survey: new and removed structures, fresh digging and new tracks, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer.
  • Files your teams already use: GeoPackage, Shapefile, GeoJSON and KMZ layers, and a PDF report in English.

Our standard

Land and assets, never people

AfriScan maps what is on the land: structures, cleared ground, excavations, tracks and vegetation. We do not identify, count or follow people, and we do not decide who is entitled to what. Satellites cannot see theft, vandalism or tapping; they show where the ground has changed, and a person decides what that change means.

A person reviews every result

Building datasets and detection models propose; a reviewer confirms, corrects and adds before anything reaches you.

Dated and credited

Every report names its imagery and its capture dates where the source gives them. Undated basemaps are never passed off as survey imagery.

Scheduled re-surveys

Imagery is captured on particular dates, so re-surveys follow a schedule agreed with you, with a change notice after each one, checked by a person.

Confidential by default

Results go only to the contacts you name. Military and other sensitive sites are masked, and nothing about your assets is published.

Satellite first, drones where they add value

Two routes to the picture, and the rules for each

Satellite and your own imagery. A survey starts from your route file and dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or the orthophotos your own teams already hold. Satellite mapping needs no drone approvals and no one near lines, roads or homes, however long the corridor.

Drone detail. Where you need centimetre detail, a drone survey in Uganda needs UCAA approval, a security clearance from the Chief of Defence Forces and district sign-off for each job. We are working towards our own Ugandan drone approvals. Until then, any drone survey we arrange is flown by a Ugandan operator under its own approvals, and we tell you which approvals the job relies on.

How we work in Uganda

National content, tenders and who delivers

Where Ugandan law reserves work for Ugandan companies, such as land surveying and environmental studies on petroleum projects, and many public tenders, the work is delivered through a Ugandan partner or joint venture that meets the rules, or as a subcontractor to your appointed consultant or contractor. Our analysis, review and reporting stay the same.

National content and procurement notes

We respond to tenders, RFQs and requests from primes and consultants. Send the documents with your request; the proposal sets out how the engagement is structured for your contract and which registrations the delivering party has in place.

Where we work

Satellite mapping across Uganda, field work within clear limits

Where we do not offer field or drone work

We map assets across Uganda from satellite imagery, which needs no one on site. We do not offer field or drone work in districts along the DRC and South Sudan borders, or in Karamoja and its neighbouring districts, and we follow current travel advice for every field visit elsewhere.

Frequently asked questions

Which widths do you measure in Uganda?

Yours. For pipelines we report the bands you set from the centreline or from the edge of the right of way, such as the 6 m and 30 m distances in the 2016 Midstream Regulations. For power lines we use the wayleave in your project’s resettlement framework, such as the 10 m right of way and 25 m of wayleave either side on a new 400 kV line. For roads we use the reserve width and building line your road authority applies. Up to six widths can be reported in one survey.

How do we know how old the imagery is?

Every report names its imagery and, where the source gives it, the capture date of each scene, so each feature in the register carries a date. Where the archive is too old for the record you need, very-high-resolution scenes can be sourced or a new capture requested; its date depends on satellite availability and weather.

Do we need drones?

Usually not. Satellite mapping covers the whole corridor and needs no drone approvals. A drone survey in Uganda needs UCAA approval, Chief of Defence Forces security clearance and a district sign-off for each job, so we keep drone work for the stretches that need centimetre detail, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires.

Will you tell us which structures are unauthorised?

No. We map what stands where, and when it first appeared on dated imagery. Whether a structure is authorised, compensated or eligible is for you, your land team and the authorities to decide.

Do you map people or households?

No. We map structures, cleared ground, excavations and tracks, never people. People and vehicles in drone imagery are blurred, and names and ID numbers stay with your census and land teams.

Do you work in the border districts and Karamoja?

We do not offer field or drone work in districts along the DRC and South Sudan borders, or in Karamoja and its neighbouring districts, and every field visit elsewhere follows current travel advice.

Know what stands inside your corridor before the next survey is due.

Send the route (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage) or the site boundary, the districts it crosses and the widths that matter: a pipeline right of way and the 6 m and 30 m bands, a wayleave corridor, a road reserve, or your own standard. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
